takeaways: Septic systems: Minnesota has no statewide septic inspection requirement at sale. Some counties, such as Chisago and Nicollet, have their own point-of-sale rules, and many have none, so ask the county and get the system inspected yourself.

A compliance certificate is generally good for three years (five for a new system), so check its date. Replacing a failing system, often a mound system in Minnesota soils, runs about $30,000 to $45,000 according to Jason.

Lake homes: state shoreland rules set building setbacks by lake class: 75 feet on general development lakes, 100 on recreational development lakes and 150 on natural environment lakes (for lots without city sewer). Counties and cities can be stricter.
"Grandfathered" docks, boathouses and decks may not be rebuilt or expanded if they're damaged. Get the permit history and ask the county or city directly before you pay a lake premium.

Radon: more than two in five Minnesota homes tested come back high. A test is cheap, and a mitigation system usually costs $1,500 to $2,500. Retest every two years with a system and about every five without.

Private wells: test for bacteria every year, nitrate every other year, and arsenic, lead and manganese at least once. Arsenic shows up in about 40% of new wells, and about 1 in 10 private wells exceeds the safe limit.

Old unsealed wells can turn up even in first-ring suburbs like Richfield, Bloomington, Edina and St. Louis Park on homes built before about 1970. Unused wells must be sealed, and a well disclosure certificate goes with the deed at closing.

"As-is" means the seller won't fix things, not that you can't inspect. Jason's advice: keep your inspection contingency, and get an independent stucco inspection on stucco homes built from about 1990 to 2010.

faq.q: Is a septic inspection required to sell a house in Minnesota?
faq.a: Not statewide. Some counties require a compliance inspection at sale and many don't, so check with the county and get your own inspection if the home has a private septic system.

faq.q: How much does radon mitigation cost in Minnesota?
faq.a: Usually $1,500 to $2,500, according to Jason; most homes can be done for under $2,500. The system is a pipe and fan that vents soil gas from under the slab above the roof.

faq.q: What should I test a private well for?
faq.a: Coliform bacteria every year, nitrate every other year, and arsenic, lead and manganese at least once, following the Minnesota Department of Health's schedule. Make testing a contingency if the seller has no recent results.

faq.q: Can I inspect a house sold as-is?
faq.a: Yes. As-is means the seller isn't making repairs, but you can still negotiate a full inspection period, which matters even more when disclosures are limited.

takeaways: With the Twin Cities median around $390,000 (as stated in the video), $750,000 is entry-level money in some neighborhoods and near the top of the market in others.

Edina (median around $600,000): $750,000 buys an updated three- or four-bedroom home, often a mid-century rambler, near 50th and France or Southdale. Areas like Country Club and Indian Hills start well over $1 million, and teardowns are common.

Linden Hills, Minneapolis: $750,000 is about the neighborhood median and buys a 1920s to 1940s bungalow or Tudor near Lake Harriet and Bde Maka Ska. You pay a lake premium for an older, often smaller home, and Minneapolis property taxes run higher.

Excelsior on Lake Minnetonka: $750,000 is entry level. It buys a home near the lake and the walkable downtown, but not on the water, where shoreline runs into the millions. White Bear Lake and Stillwater offer a similar feel on the east side.
Woodbury (median around $450,000): $750,000 buys a large, newer four- or five-bedroom home with a three-car garage, about 15 to 20 minutes from downtown Saint Paul. It's car-dependent.
Northeast Minneapolis (median in the mid-$300,000s): $750,000 can buy a fully remodeled home or a duplex near the arts district and the river. Check flood maps on riverfront blocks.
Jason's own pick: Lakeville, where his family and business are. His advice is to buy where your daily life is: Woodbury on the east side, Blaine to the north, Victoria to Maple Grove in the west.

faq.a: Usually an updated three- or four-bedroom home, often a mid-century rambler, since the Edina median is around $600,000 per the video. Neighborhoods like Country Club and Indian Hills start over $1 million.

faq.q: Can you buy a lakefront home on Lake Minnetonka for $750,000?
faq.a: Generally not. In Excelsior, $750,000 buys a home near the lake and downtown, but shoreline property there runs into the millions.

takeaways: The Green Line Extension (Southwest light rail) is set to open in 2027 after years of delays, at a final cost of about $3 billion. Eden Prairie gets four stations: Southwest Station, Town Center, Golden Triangle and City West, about 35 minutes to downtown Minneapolis.
More than $3 billion of development is built, under way or planned along the line, including more than 8,000 housing units.

Eden Prairie Center may be reimagined. A concept for the former JCPenney site includes about 750 apartments, a hotel, event space, offices and ground-floor retail. As of the video it wasn't approved, and a special tax-increment financing authority from 2025 had a deadline.

Transit-oriented apartments are already rising near the stations: Fox and the Grouse (about 400 units in two phases), City West Apartments (about 200 units, due around 2027) and Elevate at Southwest Station.

The Golden Triangle, about 1,000 acres with around 25,000 pre-pandemic jobs, is being reinvested in. The 60-acre former Danfoss site was re-guided in 2025 for a mix of up to about 2,000 homes plus retail and office space next to Southwest Station.
Eden Prairie has little land left to build outward, so growth is moving inward. The city's property tax levy has risen about 4% a year on average over the past decade, with about 6% planned for 2026.
Market as of the video (March 2026): median in the mid-$400,000s to low $500,000s, about 40 days on market and about two months of supply.

faq.q: Where are the light rail stations in Eden Prairie?
faq.a: Four Green Line Extension stations: Southwest Station (the end of the line), Town Center, Golden Triangle and City West. Service is expected to start in 2027.

faq.q: How long will the light rail take from Eden Prairie to downtown Minneapolis?
faq.a: About 35 minutes with no transfers, according to the video.

takeaways: For four years, owners with 2% and 3% mortgages stayed put because moving to a 6.5% rate raised the payment 35% to 40%. That froze the market.
In June 2026 the standoff broke without any rate cut. Twin Cities new listings jumped about 10%, metro inventory reached almost 11,000 homes, and statewide inventory topped 19,000, a seven-year high.
The reason was equity: the metro median is up about 17% since 2021, so many owners can make a bigger down payment and keep the next payment manageable even at today's rates.
Buyers absorbed the new supply: pending sales rose 9.7% and closings 10.7%, with about 5,600 homes closing in June, and the metro median reached a June record of $410,000.
Selling got harder: homes averaged 42 days on market (up from 39), and sellers received 99.6% of their original list price, down from 100%. Price honestly from day one and present the home well.
Three questions decide whether to move now: what you still owe, what you'd realistically buy next, and how your home compares with what's for sale near you.

faq.q: Should I give up a 3% mortgage rate to move?
faq.a: It depends on your equity. With Twin Cities prices up about 17% since 2021, many owners can put more down on the next home and keep the payment workable even at around 6.5%. Run the numbers with your payoff and your next home's price.

faq.q: Are home prices falling in the Twin Cities?
faq.a: No. Even with inventory at a multi-year high, the metro median reached a June record of $410,000. Homes are taking a bit longer to sell and sellers are negotiating more.

takeaways: Minneapolis ranks high for retirement, but it suits retirees who go in prepared on five things: winter, taxes, lifestyle, health care and day-to-day practicalities.
Winter is a physical, financial and social issue in retirement: black ice and falls, heating bills in older homes, and isolation when it's too cold to go out.

Minnesota taxes Social Security above certain income levels. For the 2025 tax year, benefits are fully exempt for married couples filing jointly with income up to $108,320 and single filers up to $84,490; the exemption phases out above that. The top income tax rate is 9.85%.

Health care is the strongest argument for staying: Mayo Clinic in Rochester is ranked among the best hospitals in the world, and Twin Cities hospitals like Abbott Northwestern rank highly. Check Medicare plan changes, since some insurers scaled back Minnesota plans for 2026.
Medicare Part D now caps yearly out-of-pocket prescription costs, at $2,000 in 2025 and $2,100 in 2026.
Building a social life takes effort here. 55+ communities help, and the Twin Cities has fewer of them than Sunbelt markets, though Jason finds the ones here high quality and less crowded.
Day to day, most neighborhoods need a car, though the Green Line Extension (2027) will help. MSP Airport makes winter getaways easy.

faq.a: Partly. For the 2025 tax year, Social Security is fully exempt from Minnesota tax for married couples filing jointly with income up to $108,320 and single filers up to $84,490, with the exemption phasing out above those amounts. Confirm with your tax preparer.

faq.q: Is Minneapolis a good place to retire?
faq.a: For retirees who plan for winter, taxes and building a social life, it offers excellent health care, culture, lakes and an easy airport. Jason's advice is to go in with the full picture, not just the rankings.

takeaways: Winter's length surprises people more than the cold: it can run from November through March, with short, dark days. Minnesotans lean in with outdoor rinks, cross-country skiing, ice fishing and pond hockey, and trails are cleared quickly.

The job base is broad: UnitedHealth Group, Target, Best Buy, U.S. Bank, 3M and General Mills are headquartered here, and Cargill, the largest privately held company, is based in the Minnetonka–Wayzata area.
MSP Airport is Delta's second-largest hub, with nonstop flights to most of the country in about three hours or less.

Quirks to know: Sunday liquor sales have been legal only since 2017; liquor stores are closed on Thanksgiving and Christmas; and grocery stores sell only low-alcohol beer, so wine and liquor come from separate liquor stores.
Outdoor warning sirens are tested at 1 p.m. on the first Wednesday of every month, plus twice on the statewide tornado drill day each spring.
"Minnesota nice" is real, but friendships can take time to form.

In a Minnesota home, an attached (ideally heated) garage, a mudroom and a well-plowed street matter more than newcomers expect. Market as of the video: about 11,600 metro homes for sale, a metro median around $408,000, and homes selling in about 40 days at about 99% of list price.

faq.q: Can you buy wine at grocery stores in Minnesota?
faq.a: No. Minnesota grocery stores can sell only low-alcohol beer. Wine, liquor and full-strength beer come from liquor stores, which sometimes have a separate entrance next to a grocery store.

faq.q: Why do sirens go off on the first Wednesday of the month in Minnesota?
faq.a: Most counties test their outdoor warning sirens at 1 p.m. on the first Wednesday of every month. There's also a statewide tornado drill each spring with two siren tests that day.
